items.learningObjective: Name the HIPAA term for individually identifiable health information.
items.question: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, what is the term generally used for individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or its business associate?

choices.text: Protected health information (PHI)
choices.why: Correct: HHS's summary calls this information protected health information.

choices.text: A designated record set kept by the provider
choices.why: A defined group of records, not the term for the information itself.

choices.text: A notice of privacy practices for patients
choices.why: A document telling patients how information is used.

choices.text: A business associate agreement on file
choices.why: A contract, not the name for the information.

items.rationale: HHS: "The Privacy Rule protects all 'individually identifiable health information' held or transmitted by a covered entity or its business associate, in any form or media... The Privacy Rule calls this information 'protected health information (PHI).'" The stem says "generally" because the same page records exclusions from PHI: employment records a covered entity holds as an employer, and education and certain other records subject to FERPA (20 U.S.C. 1232g). PHI is the general term, not an absolute one.

source.locator: Heading 'What Information is Protected', paragraphs 'Protected Health Information' and the FERPA/employment-records exclusion

items.learningObjective: Recognize the three kinds of covered entity.
items.question: Which of the following is one of the three types of covered entity that the HIPAA Privacy Rule applies to?

choices.text: A pharmaceutical manufacturer selling to clinics
choices.why: Not one of the covered-entity types.

choices.text: A health care clearinghouse
choices.why: Correct: health plans, health care clearinghouses, and providers that transmit health information electronically in standard transactions are covered.

choices.text: A patient's family caregiver who helps with care
choices.why: A family member is not a covered entity.

choices.text: A medical-scribe training website
choices.why: Not, by that fact alone, a covered entity.

items.rationale: The Privacy Rule applies to health plans, health care providers that transmit health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, and health care clearinghouses.

items.learningObjective: Know that treatment disclosures between providers do not require patient authorization.
items.question: A covered clinic's physician sends a patient's lab report and diagnosis to a specialist she is referring the patient to. Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, is the patient's written authorization required for this disclosure?

choices.text: Yes; written authorization is required before any disclosure between providers, even for treatment.
choices.why: The Rule permits disclosure for treatment without authorization.

choices.text: Yes, but only when the specialist practices at a different building or organization.
choices.why: Location or organization is not the test.

choices.text: No; the Rule permits covered providers to disclose PHI for treatment without authorization.
choices.why: Correct.

choices.text: No, because lab reports and diagnoses are not PHI, so the Rule does not apply to them.
choices.why: They are PHI; the reason no authorization is needed is the treatment purpose.

items.rationale: HHS: a covered entity "may use and disclose protected health information for its own treatment, payment, and health care operations activities", and "also may disclose protected health information for the treatment activities of any health care provider" - without the individual's authorization (45 CFR 164.506). Treatment expressly includes "consultation between providers regarding a patient and referral of a patient by one provider to another." This removes the authorization requirement for the disclosure; it does not exempt the disclosure from the rest of the Privacy Rule.

source.locator: FAQ answer text; also treatment definition in HHS-PR-SUMMARY 'Permitted Uses and Disclosures'

items.learningObjective: Identify a disclosure the minimum necessary standard does not apply to.
items.question: The minimum necessary standard requires reasonable efforts to limit PHI to what is needed for the purpose. Which of these is NOT subject to that standard?

choices.text: A billing office asking for more patient detail than a claim requires
choices.why: Subject to the standard.

choices.text: An administrative use of a patient's full record for an unrelated, non-treatment purpose
choices.why: Subject to the standard; not on the exception list.

choices.text: A health plan requesting a patient's complete chart for a routine payment determination
choices.why: Payment is not on the exception list, so the standard applies.

choices.text: A disclosure to a health care provider for treatment
choices.why: Correct: 45 CFR 164.502(b)(2)(i) excepts disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment.

items.rationale: HHS lists six circumstances in which "the minimum necessary requirement is not imposed": (a) disclosure to or a request by a health care provider for treatment; (b) disclosure to the individual or their personal representative; (c) use or disclosure made pursuant to an authorization; (d) disclosure to HHS for complaint investigation, compliance review or enforcement; (e) use or disclosure required by law; (f) use or disclosure required for compliance with the HIPAA Administrative Simplification Rules. Choice (d) is the one of those six present among these options - not the only exception in HIPAA.

source.locator: Heading 'Limiting Uses and Disclosures to the Minimum Necessary', the six-item exception list

items.learningObjective: Distinguish treatment from payment and health care operations.
items.question: Which activity fits the Privacy Rule's definition of 'treatment'?

choices.text: Providers coordinating one patient's care, including a referral
choices.why: Correct: treatment includes coordination of care and referral of a patient by one provider to another.

choices.text: A health plan determining premiums and coverage for its members
choices.why: That is payment.

choices.text: A clinic reviewing quality measures across all of its patients
choices.why: Quality assessment is a health care operation.

choices.text: An auditor reviewing claims for medical review and legal compliance
choices.why: Audits and legal services fall under health care operations.

items.rationale: HHS defines treatment as the provision, coordination, or management of health care and related services for an individual by one or more health care providers, including consultation between providers regarding a patient and referral of a patient by one provider to another. Payment and health care operations are separate categories.

source.locator: Heading 'Permitted Uses and Disclosures', definition of Treatment

items.learningObjective: Apply the business associate definition to an outside vendor.
items.question: A covered clinic hires an outside company to store and maintain its patients' scanned records on the company's servers. The company will not treat patients or bill for the clinic. Under HHS's description, what is the company's status, and what must the clinic have in place before giving it the records?

choices.text: Not a business associate, because it never treats patients or bills for the clinic
choices.why: Treating or billing is not the test; creating, receiving, maintaining, or transmitting PHI for the covered entity is.

choices.text: A business associate; a written contract or arrangement giving assurances must come first
choices.why: Correct: maintaining PHI on the clinic's behalf makes it a business associate, and satisfactory assurances in writing are required before disclosure.

choices.text: A business associate, but no written arrangement is needed if the vendor has a good reputation
choices.why: A written arrangement providing satisfactory assurances is required.

choices.text: A covered entity, so it needs its own patient authorizations before storing records
choices.why: Performing a function for a covered entity does not by itself make it one.

items.rationale: HHS defines a business associate as a person that performs functions or activities on behalf of a covered entity "that involve creating, receiving, maintaining, or transmitting PHI" - storing and maintaining the records is squarely 'maintaining'. HHS: the Rules "permit a covered entity to disclose PHI to a business associate if the covered entity obtains satisfactory assurances, in the form of a contract or other written arrangement... that the business associate will appropriately safeguard the information." The status turns on the vendor's role and its PHI handling, not on being an outside company: HHS is explicit that persons are "not considered business associates if their functions or services do not involve the use or disclosure of protected health information, and where any access... would be incidental, if at all."

source.locator: Headings 'What is a Business Associate?' and the satisfactory-assurances paragraph under 'Background'

items.learningObjective: Identify ICD-10-CM as the U.S. clinical modification used for diagnosis coding.
items.question: Which classification did the U.S. develop from the WHO's ICD-10 for coding diseases and medical conditions (morbidity data)?

choices.text: ICD-10-PCS, the U.S. procedure coding system
choices.why: PCS is the separate procedure system.

choices.text: The WHO's ICD-10 exactly as the WHO publishes it
choices.why: That is the base classification, not the U.S. modification.

choices.text: ICD-10-CM, the U.S. clinical modification
choices.why: Correct: NCHS is responsible for the clinical modification of ICD-10 for U.S. use.

choices.text: The Alphabetic Index used on its own
choices.why: The Index is one component of ICD-10-CM, not a system.

items.rationale: CDC describes ICD-10-CM as a standardized system used to code diseases and medical conditions (morbidity) data. NCHS is responsible for the clinical modification of ICD-10 for U.S. use; WHO owns ICD-10. CMS develops ICD-10-PCS, the procedure system.

items.question: In ICD-10-CM, which description matches the Tabular List?

choices.text: An alphabetical list of terms with their corresponding codes, used to begin a lookup
choices.why: That describes the Alphabetic Index.

choices.text: A list of each insurer's reimbursed codes and payment rules
choices.why: Not a component of the classification.

choices.text: The provider's list of diagnoses documented for one encounter
choices.why: That is documentation, not the classification.

choices.text: A structured list of codes divided into chapters by body system or condition
choices.why: Correct.

items.rationale: The Official Guidelines describe ICD-10-CM as divided into the Alphabetic Index, an alphabetical list of terms and their corresponding codes, and the Tabular List, a structured list of codes divided into chapters based on body system or condition.

source.locator: Section I.A.1 'The Alphabetic Index and Tabular List'

items.question: According to the ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines, what is the correct way to select a code for a diagnosis documented in the medical record?

choices.text: Find the term in the Alphabetic Index, then verify the code in the Tabular List
choices.why: Correct.

choices.text: Choose the code from the Alphabetic Index alone, since the Tabular List only repeats it
choices.why: The Guidelines say both must be used.

choices.text: Reuse the code assigned at the patient's previous visit for the same complaint
choices.why: Code assignment follows current documentation.

choices.text: Browse the Tabular List for a similar-looking code and assign it directly
choices.why: The lookup starts from the Index term.

items.rationale: The Guidelines direct the coder to first locate the term in the Alphabetic Index and then verify the code in the Tabular List, and state that it is essential to use both.

source.locator: Section I.B.1 'Locating a code in the ICD-10-CM'

items.learningObjective: Know when an 'unspecified' code is appropriate.
items.question: According to the ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines, when is a code titled 'unspecified' appropriate?

choices.text: When the coder cannot recall the more specific code and wants to save time
choices.why: Memory and speed are not the criteria.

choices.text: When the provider documented no diagnosis at all, as a placeholder code
choices.why: An unspecified code still reflects a documented condition; it is not a stand-in for none.

choices.text: When the record lacks enough information for a more specific code
choices.why: Correct.

choices.text: Whenever the more specific code would take longer to find in the Index
choices.why: Effort is not the criterion.

items.rationale: The Guidelines say codes titled 'unspecified' are for use when the information in the medical record is insufficient to assign a more specific code, and that they should be reported when they most accurately reflect what is known at the encounter.

source.locator: Section I.A.9.b 'Unspecified' codes (CORRECTED from I.B.18 in revision 1)

items.learningObjective: Recognize that diagnosis code assignment rests on the patient's provider's documentation.
items.question: During chart review, a non-provider nurse's intake note says the patient "seems like they have diabetes." The patient's provider has not documented a diabetes diagnosis for the encounter. Under the ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines, what is the appropriate conclusion about assigning a diabetes diagnosis code based on this note alone?

choices.text: Assign the diabetes code because the nurse's note is part of the medical record
choices.why: Diagnosis code assignment is based on the patient's provider's documentation.

choices.text: Assign an 'unspecified' diabetes code because the specific details are missing
choices.why: 'Unspecified' is for a documented diagnosis lacking detail, not one never documented by the provider.

choices.text: Assign it if the chart also lists a diabetes medication from another clinic
choices.why: Coding a diagnosis from an inferred medication link is unsupported inference.

choices.text: Do not assign it from this note alone; provider documentation is required
choices.why: Correct: diagnosis code assignment is based on the patient's provider's documentation, and diabetes is not among the defined exceptions.

items.rationale: FY2027 Section I.B.14: "Code assignment is based on the documentation by the patient's provider (i.e., physician or other qualified healthcare practitioner legally accountable for establishing the patient's diagnosis)." The same section continues: "There are a few exceptions when code assignment may be based on medical record documentation from clinicians who are not the patient's provider" - listing BMI, depth of non-pressure chronic ulcers, pressure ulcer stage, coma scale, NIH stroke scale, social determinants of health, laterality, blood alcohol level and underimmunization status, among others. A diabetes diagnosis is not among them, so this note alone cannot support the code. The rule is not that non-provider documentation can never support any code - it plainly can, for the listed exceptions.

source.locator: Section I.B.14 'Documentation by Clinicians Other than the Patient's Provider' (page 16 of 121), read with I.A.19 'Code assignment and Clinical Criteria'
